facts.text: Bring out the timpano when the dinner guests hold their breath.
facts.why: The timpano comes out while the party waits on Louis Prima, and the film never has the guests hold their breath.
facts.fix: Bring out the timpano when the dinner party is still waiting on Louis Prima.

facts.text: Timpano. The pasta drum. The room goes quiet when it's cut
facts.why: The guests react loudly, not quietly: one bite and they shout Paradise and say it is so good they should kill the cook.
facts.fix: Timpano. The pasta drum. One bite and the room shouts Paradise

facts.text: Roast pork, whole-pig style. Carried in on a board at the feast
facts.why: Nothing I could open shows a roast pig, or anything carried in on a board, at the feast.
facts.fix: Roast pork, whole-pig style. Part of the feast on the big night

facts.text: Panna cotta -- Primo's dessert, simple and perfect
facts.why: The film never shows a dessert or a panna cotta, and the plot only has the timpano, the risotto and the omelette at dawn.
facts.fix: Panna cotta -- a sweet finish after the timpano

facts.text: Primo's caffè corretto with grappa -- the brothers' nightcap in the kitchen after the big night
facts.why: No nightcap in the kitchen is shown. The brothers share an omelette at dawn, and grappa only comes up as a drink offered to settle Primo.
facts.fix: Primo's caffè corretto with grappa -- a little grappa to make you feel better, as the film says

vibe.verdict: The food and the feast order are right, and the silent omelette ending is a lovely pick. The page misses the characters and the arguments.
